A ridge is a long, narrow, raised strip — something that runs lengthwise and sits higher than the surfaces on either side of it. Think of it like the spine of a book: raised in the middle, with flat or lower areas dropping away on both sides.

That single mental image — something elevated, elongated, and narrow, with lower ground on both sides — will unlock almost every use of this word.

1. A Ridge in Nature (Landscape)

This is the most common meaning. When you look at mountains or hills, a ridge is the long, raised crest or line that runs along the top or side.

  • It is not just a single peak (that would be a summit).
  • It is a continuous elevated line, like the top edge of a tent.
  • On either side of a mountain ridge, the land slopes downward.

Imagine two hikers on opposite sides of a mountain. The ridge is the raised spine they are both climbing toward.

A ridge can be massive — stretching for hundreds of miles — or it can be a small raised strip on a hillside. What matters is the shape: long, narrow, and higher than what surrounds it.

2. A Ridge on a Roof

This is one of the most familiar everyday uses. The ridge of a roof is the highest horizontal line at the very top, where the two sloping sides of the roof meet.

  • The two sides of the roof rise upward and meet at a single line at the top.
  • That meeting line is the ridge.
  • It runs the full length of the roof, from one end to the other.

Picture a classic house roof shape — like an upside-down "V." The very tip of that V, running lengthwise, is the ridge.

3. A Ridge on a Surface

A ridge doesn't have to be a mountain or a rooftop. Any raised, narrow line on a surface can be called a ridge.

On your body:

  • Your fingerprints are made up of tiny ridges — the small raised lines that loop and swirl across your fingertips.
  • The ridge of your nose is the raised line that runs from between your eyes down to the tip.
  • The brow ridge is the bony raised edge above your eyes.

On objects:

  • A coin has ridges on its edge — small raised lines running around the rim.
  • A ribbed fabric like corduroy has ridges — small raised strips running parallel to each other.
  • A tire has ridges in its tread — raised patterns that grip the road.

The rule holds in every case: a raised, elongated strip, with lower areas on both sides.

4. A Ridge in Farming

In agriculture, a ridge is a raised strip of soil created when a farmer ploughs a field. Ploughing pushes soil into long mounds running in rows. These mounds are ridges. Between each ridge is a lower channel called a furrow.

Imagine rows of raised soil in a potato field — each raised row is a ridge.

5. A Ridge in Weather (Meteorology)

In weather science, a ridge refers to an elongated area of high atmospheric pressure stretching outward from a high-pressure system — much like a mountain ridge extends from a peak.

  • High pressure is associated with dry, clear weather.
  • When a meteorologist says a "ridge" is building over a region, they mean a stretch of high pressure is moving in, likely bringing sunny skies.

The word is used here as a direct metaphor: just as a mountain ridge is a raised strip of land, a pressure ridge is a raised strip of atmospheric pressure on a weather map.

6. A Ridge on the Ocean Floor

The ocean floor has its own ridges — called mid-ocean ridges — which are enormous underwater mountain ranges running along the ocean floor. The same logic applies: long, continuous, elevated structures rising above the surrounding ocean floor.

No matter the context, a ridge always has these qualities:

  • It is raised — higher than its surroundings.
  • It is long and narrow — not a wide plateau, not a single point.
  • It has lower areas on both sides — the ridge is the crest of something.

Whether it is a mountain spine, a rooftop peak, a fingerprint line, a farming mound, or a weather pattern — if it is a long, narrow, raised strip, it is a ridge.

• Mountain ridge — the crest of a mountain range.
  • Ridge line / ridgeline — the continuous line formed by the top of a ridge, especially in a landscape.
  • Ridge tile — a specially shaped tile used to cover and protect the ridge of a roof.
  • Ridge of high pressure — a meteorological term for a band of high-pressure air.
  • Fingerprint ridge — one of the tiny raised lines that make up a fingerprint pattern.
